nodes.label: Variables, Measurement Scales, and Population vs. Sample Structure
nodes.explanation: Assumes university entry background in arithmetic, fractions, proportions, percentages, and reading basic tables. Establishes the vocabulary and structure of tabular datasets—observational units (cases), variables, values, and tidy case-by-variable layouts—alongside the descriptive distinction between populations (size N, descriptive parameters) and samples (size n, sample statistics), explicitly leaving random sampling designs and statistical inference to later trees. Classifies variables into categorical (qualitative) and quantitative (discrete vs. continuous), and develops Stevens' four measurement scales—nominal, ordinal, interval, and ratio—connecting each scale to its permissible comparisons and arithmetic operations (equality, ordering, differences, and meaningful ratios relative to a true zero). Uses concrete datasets to confront core misconceptions: treating numeric ID codes, ZIP codes, or Likert-scale ranks as ratio quantities; confusing discrete quantitative counts with categorical variables; and forming ratios on interval scales such as Celsius temperatures. Enables the learner to audit a dataset's structure, classify every variable by type and scale, and determine which numerical and graphical summaries are mathematically legitimate before computing anything. Leaves frequency tables, plots, and numerical summary formulas to subsequent lessons.

nodes.label: Frequency Distributions, Grouped Classes, and Ogives
nodes.explanation: Builds on variable types and measurement scales (and proportional relationships from entry background) to organize raw univariate data into structured frequency summaries. Develops ungrouped frequency, relative frequency, and cumulative frequency (and cumulative relative frequency) tables for categorical and discrete quantitative variables, verifying that relative frequencies sum to 1 (up to rounding) and explaining why cumulative frequencies require at least an ordinal scale. Develops grouped frequency distributions for continuous or wide-range quantitative data—distinguishing class limits from exact class boundaries (resolving boundary assignment conventions consistently), computing class midpoints and class widths, weighing bin-count trade-offs (oversmoothing vs. noise, using heuristics such as Sturges' rule or √n as starting guides rather than rigid laws), and introducing frequency density (relative frequency divided by class width) when class widths are unequal. Constructs and reads cumulative frequency polygons (ogives) plotted at upper class boundaries to estimate running proportions below a threshold and approximate inverse thresholds. Enables the learner to build clean ungrouped and grouped frequency tables, verify density consistency across unequal bins, and extract threshold proportions from ogives. Leaves graphical shape diagnostics via histograms and exact quantile definitions to the next lessons.

nodes.label: Graphical Displays of Univariate Data: Bar Charts, Histograms, and Dotplots
nodes.explanation: Builds on frequency distributions and grouped classes to construct, read, and critique standard univariate plots. Matches chart type to variable scale: bar charts and Pareto charts for categorical data (with separated bars and category ordering reflecting nominal vs. ordinal structure) versus histograms, frequency polygons, dotplots, and stem-and-leaf displays for quantitative data (with contiguous numeric intervals). Establishes the area principle as the central bridge in quantitative graphics—showing why unequal-width histograms must plot frequency density rather than raw counts on the vertical axis so bar area stays proportional to relative frequency. Trains qualitative shape reading directly from displays—identifying unimodal, bimodal, and multimodal structure, approximate symmetry, right (positive) and left (negative) skewness, gaps, clusters, and apparent outliers—and diagnoses deceptive visual practices such as truncated vertical axes on bar charts, 2D/3D pictogram area distortion, and extreme bin-width choices that conceal bimodality or manufacture spurious spikes. Enables the learner to select and construct an appropriate univariate chart, read distribution shape accurately, and critique misleading displays. Leaves boxplots (which require quartiles and fences) and bivariate scatterplots to later lessons.

nodes.label: Measures of Center: Mean, Median, Mode, and Weighted or Trimmed Means
nodes.explanation: Builds on variable types and measurement scales (assuming high-school algebra) to summarize central location and compare estimator resistance. Introduces summation notation ∑_{i=1}^n x_i and its linearity properties, defines the sample arithmetic mean x̄ = (1/n) ∑ x_i and population mean μ, and proves the balance-point identity ∑ (x_i − x̄) = 0. Develops the sample median (handling odd and even n cleanly after sorting), the mode and modal class, the weighted arithmetic mean x̄_w = (∑ w_i x_i)/(∑ w_i) (applied both to combining subgroup means and to approximating the mean of grouped data via class midpoints), and α-trimmed and Winsorized means as structured compromises between the mean and median. Connects measurement scale directly to valid summaries (mode for nominal; median and mode for ordinal; mean for interval and ratio) and analyzes robustness via concrete outlier perturbations, demonstrating why a single extreme observation can shift x̄ arbitrarily while leaving the median and trimmed mean stable. Enables the learner to compute exact and grouped centers, combine subgroup averages without committing the unweighted-average-of-averages error, and choose between classical and resistant centers. Leaves geometric/harmonic means to optional enrichment and measures of spread to the next lesson.

nodes.label: Geometric and Harmonic Means for Growth Rates and Ratios
nodes.explanation: Optional enrichment building on arithmetic and weighted means (assuming logarithms and roots from high-school algebra) to handle multiplicative and rate-based ratio data where the arithmetic mean gives the wrong summary. Defines the geometric mean G = (∏_{i=1}^n x_i)^{1/n} = exp((1/n) ∑ ln x_i) for positive multiplicative factors (such as compound annual growth factors 1 + r_t, ratios, and index numbers) and the harmonic mean H = n / ∑ (1/x_i) for averaging rates when the numerator quantity is held fixed (such as speeds over equal distances or prices per unit at equal expenditure), distinguishing fixed-numerator from fixed-denominator rate averaging via weighted means. Proves the AM–GM–HM inequality H ≤ G ≤ A explicitly for n = 2 (with equality iff values are equal) and states and checks it for general positive datasets, explaining why the arithmetic mean overstates compound growth when returns fluctuate. Enables the learner to select among arithmetic, weighted, geometric, and harmonic means in applied rate and growth problems and explain why an arithmetic average of percentage returns misstates cumulative growth.

nodes.label: Quantiles, Five-Number Summaries, Boxplots, and Outlier Fences
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes univariate graphical displays and ordering/median concepts (also leveraging ogives from the earlier frequency-table ancestor) to summarize position, resistant spread, and outliers. Defines p-quantiles and percentiles for 0 < p < 1, explicitly contrasting common discrete-sample conventions (nearest-rank vs. linear interpolation) and applying a consistent rule to compute quartiles Q_1, Q_2, Q_3, the five-number summary (min, Q_1, Q_2, Q_3, max), and the interquartile range IQR = Q_3 − Q_1, while connecting sample quantiles visually to inverse reads on an ogive. Develops Tukey's inner fences (Q_1 − 1.5·IQR and Q_3 + 1.5·IQR) and outer fences (Q_1 − 3·IQR and Q_3 + 3·IQR) to flag mild and extreme outliers, emphasizing that flagged points require domain investigation rather than automatic deletion. Constructs standard and modified (outlier-marking) boxplots—paying careful attention to stopping whiskers at the most extreme non-outlier observations rather than at the fence values themselves—and uses side-by-side boxplots to compare multiple groups in center, spread, asymmetry, and outliers, while contrasting boxplots with histograms/dotplots to show that boxplots conceal bimodality and internal gaps. Enables the learner to compute quantiles and IQR, flag outliers via Tukey fences, and interpret side-by-side boxplots accurately.

nodes.label: Measures of Spread: Variance, Standard Deviation, MAD, and Coefficient of Variation
nodes.explanation: Builds on summation notation and arithmetic means to quantify variability around the center. Introduces the range and diagnoses its extreme sensitivity to outliers and sample size, defines the mean absolute deviation MAD = (1/n) ∑ |x_i − x̄|, and develops population variance σ² = (1/N) ∑ (x_i − μ)², sample variance s² = (1/(n − 1)) ∑ (x_i − x̄)², and standard deviations σ and s (highlighting why taking the square root restores the original measurement units). Explains the n − 1 denominator conceptually through the linear constraint ∑ (x_i − x̄) = 0 leaving n − 1 independent deviations (degrees of freedom) and notes that formal proof of unbiasedness E[s²] = σ² belongs to Statistical Inference. Proves the algebraic identity ∑ (x_i − x̄)² = ∑ x_i² − n x̄² from summation linearity, demonstrates its shortcut use alongside the crucial numerical-stability warning about catastrophic cancellation when values are large relative to their spread, and computes grouped-data variance approximations. Introduces the dimensionless coefficient of variation CV = s/x̄ to compare relative spread across datasets with different units or scales, explicitly enforcing its domain restriction to strictly positive ratio-scale variables. Enables the learner to compute and interpret variance, standard deviation, MAD, and CV, and verify scale validity.

nodes.label: Linear Rescaling, Standardization, and z-Scores
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes quantiles/IQR and variance/standard deviation to analyze how linear transformations y_i = a x_i + b affect every descriptive summary and to place observations on a common dimensionless scale. Proves directly from definitions that location summaries (mean, median, and quantiles when a > 0, with quantile order reversing when a < 0) transform as a·L(x) + b, spread summaries in original units (SD, MAD, IQR, range) transform as |a|·S(x) and are shift-invariant, and variance scales by a², applying these rules to unit conversions (such as °C to °F or currency rescaling) without recomputing from raw data. Defines standardization z_i = (x_i − x̄)/s (or (x_i − μ)/σ) for s > 0, proves directly that the standardized dataset always has mean 0 and standard deviation 1 regardless of original units, and uses z-scores to compare relative standing across heterogeneous distributions and detect unusual observations (contrasting |z| > 2 or |z| > 3 heuristics against IQR fences on skewed data). Explicitly dispels the common misconception that standardizing a dataset makes it symmetric or bell-shaped: linear rescaling preserves exact distribution shape. Enables the learner to predict rescaled summaries instantaneously, compute and interpret z-scores, and compare relative position across scales.

nodes.label: Quantitative Distribution Shape, Skewness, and Summary Selection
nodes.explanation: Builds on linear rescaling and z-scores (together with histogram and boxplot representations from earlier ancestors) to move from visual impressions of shape to quantitative diagnostics and principled summary choice. Formalizes symmetry, positive (right) and negative (left) skewness, tail heaviness, and multimodality across histograms, boxplots, and numerical summaries. Evaluates the mean-median-mode ordering heuristic (typically mean > median for right-skewed unimodal data) while exhibiting concrete discrete/multimodal counterexamples where the rule fails so learners treat it as a diagnostic clue rather than a theorem. Introduces scale-free quantitative shape indices: Pearson's second skewness coefficient 3(x̄ − median)/s, Bowley's quartile skewness (Q_3 + Q_1 − 2Q_2)/IQR, and the sample third standardized moment g_1 = (1/n) ∑ z_i³ (alongside the standard adjusted version and a brief conceptual note on fourth standardized moments z_i⁴ capturing tail weight/kurtosis), verifying their invariance under positive linear transformations. Synthesizes these diagnostics into a decision protocol for reporting center and spread—mean and SD for roughly symmetric, outlier-free distributions versus median (or trimmed mean) and IQR for skewed or heavy-tailed distributions. Enables the learner to quantify asymmetry, interpret skewness signs and magnitudes, and defend summary choices.

nodes.label: Chebyshev's Inequality and the Empirical Rule
nodes.explanation: Builds on quantitative distribution shape and z-scores to bound and approximate how much of a dataset lies within k standard deviations of the mean. Proves Chebyshev's inequality directly for any finite dataset—for every k > 1, at least the fraction 1 − 1/k² of observations satisfy |x_i − μ| < kσ (equivalently |z_i| < k)—using the elementary variance lower bound ∑ (x_i − μ)² ≥ ∑_{|x_i − μ| ≥ kσ} k² σ² without requiring probability axioms, and notes the corresponding sample-SD bound. Contrasts this distribution-free worst-case guarantee (at least 75% within 2σ, 88.9% within 3σ) with the Empirical Rule (approximately 68%, 95%, and 99.7% within 1, 2, and 3 standard deviations), emphasizing that the Empirical Rule is an empirical/normal-model approximation licensed ONLY for unimodal, roughly symmetric, bell-shaped distributions (leaving exact normal-density integration to Probability). Trains learners to compute interval coverage bounds, estimate minimum/maximum counts outside a given threshold, and diagnose when applying the Empirical Rule to strongly skewed, heavy-tailed, or bimodal data produces severe errors while Chebyshev remains valid. Enables the learner to select and justify the valid concentration bound from observed distribution shape.

nodes.label: Two-Way Contingency Tables, Conditional Distributions, and Simpson's Paradox
nodes.explanation: Builds directly on categorical measurement scales (and proportional relationships from entry background) to analyze bivariate categorical data without needing quantitative spread or correlation machinery. Constructs r × c contingency tables and extracts joint relative frequencies, row and column marginal distributions, and row-conditioned vs. column-conditioned distributions, emphasizing the critical distinction between P(A | B) and P(B | A) in empirical table form (denominator selection). Visualizes categorical association via side-by-side and 100% stacked bar charts, defines descriptive independence (identical conditional distributions across conditioning groups) versus descriptive association, and computes basic 2×2 comparative summaries—proportion difference and descriptive relative risk—while explicitly leaving chi-square tests, p-values, and formal probability axioms to Probability and Statistical Inference. Develops Simpson's paradox in full numerical detail: demonstrating how a positive association within every stratum of a lurking/confounding variable can reverse when tables are aggregated due to imbalanced subgroup weights, and diagnosing why pooled percentages mislead. Enables the learner to read and construct conditional tables, detect categorical association, and expose confounding via stratified contingency tables.

nodes.label: Scatterplots, Sample Covariance, and Pearson Correlation
nodes.explanation: Builds on linear rescaling and z-scores to summarize bivariate quantitative data {(x_i, y_i)}_{i=1}^n. Trains systematic reading of scatterplots—identifying explanatory vs. response roles where appropriate, form (linear vs. curved), direction, strength, clusters, and bivariate outliers or high-leverage points. Defines sample covariance s_{xy} = (1/(n − 1)) ∑ (x_i − x̄)(y_i − ȳ), interpreting each term geometrically via the four quadrants centered at (x̄, ȳ), and diagnoses covariance's main weakness: its magnitude depends on arbitrary measurement units. Defines Pearson's correlation coefficient r = s_{xy}/(s_x s_y) = (1/(n − 1)) ∑ z_{x,i} z_{y,i} (for s_x, s_y > 0), proves −1 ≤ r ≤ 1 directly via the elementary nonnegative quadratic ∑ (z_{y,i} − t z_{x,i})² ≥ 0 (or finite Cauchy-Schwarz) with equality iff all points lie on a non-horizontal/non-vertical line, and proves invariance of r under positive linear rescaling of x or y (and sign reversal under negative scaling) plus symmetry r(x, y) = r(y, x). Confronts four essential pitfalls: r measures only linear association (r ≈ 0 on symmetric parabolas), r is non-resistant to a single leverage outlier, aggregating subgroups can distort r (ecological/lurking effects), and correlation never implies causation. Enables the learner to compute and interpret s_{xy} and r and diagnose when r misrepresents a scatterplot.

nodes.label: Spearman's Rank Correlation and Monotonic Association
nodes.explanation: Builds on Pearson correlation to measure monotonic association for ordinal variables, skewed quantitative data with outliers, and nonlinear monotone relationships. Explains rank transformation of paired data—assigning midranks (average ranks) whenever tied values occur—and defines Spearman's rank correlation ρ_s as Pearson's correlation coefficient computed on the ranked pairs (R(x_i), R(y_i)). Derives the classic shortcut formula ρ_s = 1 − (6 ∑ d_i²)/(n(n² − 1)) (where d_i = R(x_i) − R(y_i)) for the no-ties case from the sum and sum-of-squares of 1, …, n, explicitly proving why the shortcut becomes inaccurate when ties are present and requiring direct Pearson calculation on midranks in tied datasets. Establishes invariance of ρ_s under any strictly increasing transformation of x or y, and contrasts ρ_s against Pearson's r on diagnostic cases: strictly increasing nonlinear curves (ρ_s = 1 while r < 1), datasets contaminated by an extreme outlier (ρ_s stable while r swings dramatically), and non-monotonic U-shaped patterns where both r and ρ_s are near zero despite strong dependence. Enables the learner to compute ρ_s with and without ties and choose appropriately between Pearson's r and Spearman's ρ_s.

nodes.label: Descriptive Least-Squares Regression Line, Residuals, and R²
nodes.explanation: Builds on scatterplots, covariance, and Pearson correlation to fit and evaluate a descriptive linear trendline ŷ = b_0 + b_1 x minimizing the sum of squared vertical residuals SSE = ∑ (y_i − b_0 − b_1 x_i)². Derives b_1 = s_{xy}/s_x² = r (s_y/s_x) and b_0 = ȳ − b_1 x̄ algebraically by completing the square (making the derivation fully self-contained without multivariable calculus, while noting equivalence to the normal equations), and proves that the fitted line passes through (x̄, ȳ) and its residuals e_i = y_i − ŷ_i satisfy ∑ e_i = 0 and ∑ x_i e_i = 0. Expresses the trendline in standardized units z_ŷ = r z_x to explain regression toward the mean and why switching the roles of x and y produces a different line (warning against algebraically inverting ŷ on x). Proves the algebraic variance decomposition SST = SSR + SSE and derives R² = SSR/SST = r² as the fraction of total y-variation captured by the linear fit. Trains residual-plot diagnostics—spotting systematic curvature, funnel-shaped spread, vertical outliers, and high-leverage influential points—and warns against extrapolation outside the observed x-range. Leaves probabilistic regression models, confidence intervals for slopes, and hypothesis testing strictly to Statistical Inference.

nodes.label: Exploratory Re-expression: Log and Power Transformations
nodes.explanation: Optional enrichment synthesizing distribution skewness and descriptive least-squares trendlines (assuming logarithms and exponents from high-school algebra) to re-express skewed or curved quantitative data for clearer exploration. Introduces Tukey's ladder of powers (…, −1, −1/2, ln, 1/2, 1, 2, …) for strictly positive variables, demonstrating how concave transformations (√x, ln x, −1/x) pull in right tails to tame strong positive skewness and stabilize spread across side-by-side groups, while convex powers (x²) tame left skewness. Applies semi-log (ln y vs. x) and log-log (ln y vs. ln x) re-expressions to linearize exponential trends y ≈ a b^x and power-law trends y ≈ a x^p, fitting descriptive OLS lines on the transformed scale and validating adequacy via residual plots. Carefully addresses back-transformation interpretation—showing how a slope in a log-log fit represents an elasticity (percentage-change ratio) and warning that exp(mean(ln x)) recovers the geometric mean rather than the arithmetic mean of x. Enables the learner to select, apply, validate, and accurately back-interpret exploratory log and power transformations.
